slides.title: From chromatin footprints to gene regulatory networksReproducible methods for integrative regulatory genomics
slides.notes_text:
Good morning, and thank you for being here.
Today I’ll present my dissertation, “From chromatin footprints to gene regulatory networks.”
The central goal of this work is to develop reproducible methods that move from open chromatin, to TF-binding prediction, and finally to link target genes.

slides.title: A simple view of transcriptional regulation
slides.notes_text: As everyone in this room know, transcription is a fundamental process in biology. Just a quick reminder: transcription happens at open chromatin.  It starts with transcription factors binding to enhancers or promoters and help recruit co-activators and ultimately RNA polymerase to initiate transcription.

slides.title: Transcription factors recognize specific DNA sequence motifs
slides.notes_text: But TFs do not bind DNA randomly. They recognize different short DNA sequence patterns called motifs such as shown in here. You can appreciate here that Different types of TFs prefer different sequences to bind. There are public database such as JASPAR and HOCOMOCO that collect thousands of known motifs that have already been discovered. However, a lot of TFs binding patterns are still unknown.

slides.title: TF motifs cluster into related families
slides.notes_text: On the other hand, many different TFs can recognize very similar motifs as shown in from the JASPAR collection. I highlighted some of the large TF families, which can contain dozens of members.

slides.title: TF binding extends beyond canonical motifs
slides.notes_text: To make the story even more complex, TFs do not always bind to their canonical motifs. It is well known that TFs can bind slightly different sequences called motif variants, or they can bind cooperatively with other TFs to create new binding sites called composite sites, Alternatively, they can be recruited by other TFs to completely different genomic loci.

slides.title: TF binding is dynamic and cell-type specific
slides.notes_text: Furthermore, TF binding is cell type specific and highly dynamic. The same TFs can bind to completely different genomic regions in different cell types. And even within the same cell type, their binding can change between biological conditions. Therefore, a static motif matching cannot predict the actual TF binding.

slides.title: Protein-specific assays provide direct evidence of TF binding
slides.notes_text: As a result, people have developed many different techniques to detect actual TF binding. Here are three major assays, ChIP-seq, CUT&Run and CUT&Tag, all requiring specific antibodies to recognize the TFs. While ChIP-seq involves crosslinking and pulldown of fragmented DNA, CUT&Run and CUT&Tag use nuclease to cut native DNA near where TFs bind.  While these techniques are fundamental in helping us understand how TF bind to DNA and regulate transcription, they are technically challenging and require high quality antibodies that are not available for many TFs. They are time-consuming, labor intensive and expensive, and you can only study one TF at a time.

slides.title: ATAC-seq maps open chromatin
slides.notes_text:
So we need a more scalable way to study TF binding.  That brings us to ATAC-seq. ATAC-seq take advantage of the simple fact that transcription happens at open chromatin where DNA is not protected by the nucleosomes. 
It uses Tn5 transposes to cut and insert specific primers into these easily accessible genomic regions Then it uses PCR to amply out these open chromatin regions.
These amplified fragments are subjected to HTS, mapped back to the reference genome, allowing us to identify highly accessible regions represented as peaks.

slides.title: ATAC-seq footprinting reveals protected TF-binding sites
slides.notes_text:
But there is a twist. Within the open chromatin region, if a TF is bound, it protects the exact site where it binds from Tn5 cutting, causing a dip in the middle of the Peak, almost look like a footprint.
Here is an actual example of the aggregated footprints around FOS motifs across the genomic from ATAC analysis of HepG2 human liver cancer cells . You can appreciate the high signal on either side of the motif, but a clear drop in signal in the motif center, indicating strong binding at these sites. In contrast, no dips are detected at the ## motif sites, suggesting little binding by this TF in this cell line. You can actually compute a footprint by dividing the flank signals to the depth of the footprints, which reflect the relative binding strength of each TFs. As a result, from a single ATAC experiment, you can predict global TF binding across the genome, making it a very simple yet powerful technique that is widely used by many labs.

slides.title: Gaps in existing ATAC-seq footprinting tools
slides.notes_text:
A number of tools are already available to perform footprinting. However, they each have their drawbacks as listed here. 
Therefore, we set out to develop a new framework called fp-tools to extend existing methods to support de novo motif discovery, biological-replicate analysis, single-cell workflows, and improved computational efficiency.

slides.title: fp-tools provides an end-to-end bulk and pseudobulk workflow
slides.notes_text:
Here is the overall fp-tools workflow, which for the interest of time I will not bore you with details.
But briefly,  fp-tools can process both bulk ATAC-seq or single-cell ATAC-seq.
Both type of data will go through the same core processing steps  as listed here.
From there, fp-tools can perform differential footprinting, de novo motif discovery, revealing biologically important TFs and discovering novel TF binding sites.

slides.title: Differential footprinting highlights TF activity changes between conditions
slides.notes_text:
Here is what you get after running fp-tools on bulk ATAC data:
In this example of comparing a leukemia cell line K562 and a liver cancer HepG2 ATAC from Encode, which in case you don’t know is a public genomics source. 
Here we have two cell types, each with biological replicates.
On the left shown in both waterfall and volcano plots, fp tools revealed the top differential motifs for each cell type. And on the right, we can directly inspect the aggregated footprint profiles behind those statistics, clearly seeing the differences in binding strengths between the two cell lines for each TF.
Importantly, the fp-tool output is fully interactive. As you can see here, you can hover and click on any TF on either plots to see their aggregated footprint patterns. 
You can also use dropdown buttons to select specific motifs
You can select different replicates to show. You can change colors and line thickness. Most importantly, you can download everything in a full editable SVG file for publication! 
 HNF4A and ONECUT2 are stronger in HepG2, while GATA-family footprints are stronger in K562.

slides.title: Single-cell footprints recover cell-type-specific TF programs
slides.notes_text:
Here is an example of analyzing a public single cell ATAC data containing three major immune cell types: B cells, monocytes, and T/NK cells.
Fp-tools is able to identify cell-type specific footprint signatures for each cell type: 
STAT6 and FOSB are enriched in B cells.
CEBPA, IRF8, and RELA are enriched in Mnocotypes
And ZNF683, NR4A1, and SMAD3 are enriched in T/NK cells

slides.title: B-cell footprint signatures highlight STAT6 and FOSB
slides.notes_text:
Fp tools also allows you to visualize the activity of each TF in UMAP
Here, STAT6 and FOSB show stronger footprint signals in the B-cell cluster.

slides.title: Monocyte footprint signatures highlight CEBPA, IRF8, and RELA
slides.notes_text: Here are IRF8, and RELA are enriched in monocyte

slides.title: T/NK-cell footprints highlight ZNF683, NR4A1, and SMAD3
slides.notes_text: NR4A1, and SMAD3 in T/NK cells

slides.title: De novo motif discovery finds patterns missing from reference databases
slides.notes_text:
Importantly, fp-tools can also discover previously unknown TF motifs. 
As you can see, up to 8% of footprotints detected by fp-tools do not match any motifs in the public databases.

slides.title: De novo motifs show clear footprint signatures in K562 and HepG2
slides.notes_text: Importantly, these newly discovered motifs show strong clear aggregated footprint profiles, suggesting that these are truly active TF binding sites.

slides.title: fp-tools runs faster and uses less memory
slides.notes_text:
We also significantly improved the computational efficiency of the workflow.
Compared to TOBIAS, on which fp-tools is based on, fp-tools runs almost twice as fast and requires nearly half of the memory.

slides.title: The fp-tools browser interface makes reproducible workflows easier to use
slides.notes_text:
Finally, we made sure fp-tools is accessible to everyone with or without any coding background.
Through this browser interface, Users can simply select an analysis, load an example or select their own files, start the run, and get the results!
Importantly, the GUI aunches the same reproducible workflow used by the command line, so you are not punished for lacking coding proficiency!

slides.notes_text: Now I will introduce CraftGRN.

slides.title: TF binding is dynamic and cell-type specific
slides.notes_text: As I explained earlier, TF binding is dynamic and cell-type specific.

slides.title: TF binding extends beyond canonical motifs
slides.notes_text: TFs bind to both canonical and non-canonical sites.

slides.title: HNF4A binding extends beyond canonical motif matches
slides.notes_text:
Here is an example showing detected HNF4A binding sites in HPAF-II pancreatic cancer cells using Cut&Tag.
As you can see, the majority of the HNF4A binding sites do not contain canonical HNF4A binding motifs. 
Thus, motif/footprint alone are not sufficient for predicting actual TF binding sites.

slides.title: Existing computational approaches for TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
To address this issue, several supervised learning methods such as EPCOT have been developed to predict TF binding using existing TF-binding data. E
However, because as I mentioned earlier, many TFs do not have published binding data. Even for those that have public binding data, they are usually limited to a few cell lines. Thus, these supervised learning methods can only predict TF bindings on on limited numbers of TFs and have to generalize TF binding to new cell types that are plagued with inaccuracies. 
Because the computational intensive nature of these methods, these methods can only predict at around one-kilobase resolution, rather than at precise footprint level. 
Finally, these methods are so complex that only a skilled bioinformatician lilke me with access to high end server  is able to implement them.

slides.title: CraftGRN Module 1 assigns candidate TFs to footprinted sites
slides.notes_text:
Instead of relying on existing mismatched data, CraftGRN uses matched ATAC-seq and RNA-seq across the same biological conditions.
First, we use fp-tools to process ATAC-seq data to detect and score all the footprints across the genome. 
We then compare the footprint activity with each TF’s expression across conditions, under the assumption that if a TF truly binds to a specific genomic locus, its binding activities should correlate with its expression fluctuation across conditions.

slides.title: TF motifs cluster into related families
slides.notes_text: However, one of the technical issue we faced is that different TFs can recognize very similar motifs.

slides.title: Redundant footprint calls are merged before TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
As a result, the same footprint region is often matched to many TF motifs, and there is huge variation between regions with some regions matching to many TFs, others only matching to only a single motif. 
However, it is also true some TFs bind next to each other in separate motifs, so we also have to take care to not merge motifs that are functional distinct. 
 
By utilizing motif scores as a guide, we were able to develop an optimized strategy that collapse truly redundant footprints.

slides.title: Consolidation reduces redundancy and reveals more diverse TF families
slides.notes_text:
Here I compare the top 100 differential footproints before and after collapsing. 
As you can see, Before consolidation, the top TFs were dominated by a handful of large TF families. 
After consolidation, a much broader collection of TF families are represented.
This correction thus significantly reduced bias caused by TF redundancy.

slides.title: CraftGRN performs consistently across pancreatic TF-binding datasets
slides.notes_text:
Fo the interest of time, I will not belabor all the other technical optimization that we performed to optimize CrafGRN, instead show you how our final pipeline stacks against the state-of-art ,deep-learning method EPCOT. 
For benchmarking, we compared CraftGRN and Epcot predictions against MAFF Cut&Tag in HPAF-II produced in our own lab and a published HNF4G ChIP-seq in AsPC1 from another lab, as ground truth.
As you can see from these curves, CraftGRN in green performs comparable to or better than EPCOT in grey in terms of precision–recall rates. 
On the bottom here, we plotted the percent of true positive and false positive for the top predicted binding sites, agains showing higher accuracies in CraftGRN predictions.

slides.title: CraftGRN performs consistently across pancreatic TF-binding datasets
slides.notes_text: The same patterns hold for two addition HNF4A Cut&Tag and KLF5 ChIIPseq in HPAFII cells.

slides.title: CraftGRN preferentially recovers stronger TF-binding events
slides.notes_text:
Importantly, the corrected predicted TFBS by CraftGRN represented in solid orange lines here showed much strong actual binding signals compared to the TFBS missed by CraftGRN represented by dotted orange line.
In contrast, there is much less difference in signal between correctly and incorrectly predicted sites by EPCOT.
So CraftGRN preferentially recovers the stronger binding events as determined by experiments, while missing the weaker less confident sites.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported TF-binding sites across TFs and cell lines
slides.notes_text:
Here I show a set of representative genomic tracks comparing CraftGRN, Epcot predictions to experimentally detected binding sites for HNF4A in AsPC1, KLF5 in HPAF-II, and FOSL2 in HPAC.
As you can appreciated, Across these loci, CraftGRN predictions closely match the experimentally detected binding sites, while EPCOT tends to produce more false positive predictions, likely due to their training on unrelated cell types.

slides.title: CraftGRN performs well in an independent T-cell dataset
slides.notes_text:
We want to make sure that CraftGRN don’t just work on data we produced. So we downloaded a published paired ATAC and RNAseq datasets for T-cells and performed the same head-to-head comparisons between CraftGRN And Epcot.
Again in this completely independent dataset, CraftGRN is comparable to or better than EPCOT in ROC performance.
These results indicate that CraftGRN performance is stable across datasets.

slides.title: CraftGRN covers more TFs with lower computational cost
slides.notes_text:
Beyond prediction accuracy, we also compared computational practicality.
As you can see, CraftGRN runs much faster on CPU alone, requires less memory, and can predict the binding patterns for any expressed TFs. 
EPCOT can benefit from GPU acceleration, but its outputs remain limited to the TFs supported by the pretrained model.
So Module 1 combines broader TF coverage, lower computational cost, and competitive or improved prediction performance.

slides.notes_text:
Module 1 tells us where a TF is likely to bind.
CraftGRN Module 2 asks the next question: which genes are that TF likely to regulate from the genomic loci?

slides.title: Experimental methods for linking TF-binding sites to target genes
slides.notes_text:
Experimentally, there are two major types of evidence that people generally use to identify target genes.
One is TF perturbation followed by RNA-seq. We knock down, knock out, or overexpress a TF and look for genes that change. But these experiments are time-consuming and costly, and the expression changes can include both direct and indirect effects. A real target can also be missed if regulation depends on multiple TFs, if another TF compensates, or if we measure at the wrong time point.
The other is 3D chromatin interaction data, such as Hi-C or HiChIP. These assays can provide evidence of physical contact, but they are also resource-intensive, their resolution can be generally very low (often ~5kb), and physical contacts do not necessarily imply functional regulation.
That is why computational methods combine different types of evidence to predict target genes are needed.

slides.title: Existing computational methods for linking TFBS to target genes
slides.notes_text:
Computationally, there are several common strategies.
The simplest is proximity—for example, linking a binding site to the nearest gene or to genes within a TSS window. This is easy to apply, but it is often wrong as Enhancers don’t always regulate the closest genes.
A second approach such as ABC and ENCODE-rE2G uses 3D contact information or regulatory priors. Basically combining Hi-C and HiChIP physical-contact information with RNAseq to predict enhancer–gene relationships. 
A third Co-accessibility approach performs under the assumption that enhancers and promoters show coordinated chromatin changes across cells or samples should regulate each other. 
Finally, Integrated models such as Taiji, GRaNIE, and SCENIC+ combine accessibility, expression, motif, and other regulatory evidence. 
However, our experiences in implementing these methods have left us disappointed with their inaccuracies.
We therefore set out to develop our own method.

slides.title: CraftGRN Module 2 uses proximity and correlation to predict target genes
slides.notes_text:
Module 2 begins with the TF-binding sites predicted by Module 1.
For each site, we identify nearby candidate genes within a user-defined genomic window. If three-dimensional interaction information is available, it can be used as an additional prior.
Across matched biological conditions, we then ask two questions: does target-gene expression track with TF expression, and does it also track with the footprint activities for that TF?
When both relationships provide support, the TF–binding-site–gene relationship is retained as a predicted TF–target gene link.
We then evaluated whether these predicted targets respond in independent TF-perturbation experiments.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers perturbation-supported SOX9 and KLF5 targets
slides.notes_text:
Again without boring you through the series of optimization steps we performed, here is the final benchmarking results comparing CraftGRN to two state-of-art target gene prediction methods, Tajji and GRaNIE. 
In contrast to the low precision rates of these two existing methods, CraftGRN in green is able to identify experimentally supported target genes for SOX9 and AsPC1 in two different PDAC cell lines.
Importantly, the target gene confidence score calculated by CraftGRN tracks with the magnitude of log2 fold change from genetic silencing as determined by actual RNAseq, with top 100 scored predicted target genes showing more average expression decrease compared to top 1000 scored target genes. 
Panels C and D summarize the predicted networks. The central red node is SOX9 or KLF5, the blue boxes are additional TFs, and the gray circles are genes.
Importantly, CraftGRN not only accurately predicted target genes for individual TFs, it predicts target genes for all expressed TFs, thus allowing us to build gene regulatory networks. 
By building these GRNs, we are able to find other TFs that work together with SOX9 or KLF5 in co-regulating these target genes, thus identifying biologically meaning regulatory edges for further investigation. 
So for the experimental biologists in the room, CraftGRN can not only help you generate a list of potential target genes to validate for your favorite TF, it can also help you find its friends and collaborators, basically giving you clues on other relevant TFs you might want to consider.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers IRF4-responsive targets in an independent T-cell dataset
slides.notes_text: Next, we tested CrafGRN Module 2 against an independent T-cell dataset,  this time with IRF4 overexpression. Again, in the ROC and precision–recall curves, CraftGRN clearly outperforms Taiji and GRaNIE. On the right, you can see the top CraftGRN predictions are increasingly enriched for genes that are upregulated after IRF4, whereas the other methods show no such trends.

slides.title: IRF4, BATF, RUNX3, and T-bet converge on shared T-cell target genes
slides.notes_text: Here is CraftGRN-predicted top IRF4 regulatory network, IRF4 is predicted to work closely with BATF, RUNX3, and TBX21 (better know as T-bet), matching existing knowledge.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.notes_text:
To summarize, this work makes three connected contributions.
First, fp-tools provides reproducible and efficient ATAC-seq footprinting for bulk and single-cell data.
Second, CraftGRN Module 1 combines footprints, motifs, and TF expression to predict condition-specific TF-binding sites.
Third, CraftGRN Module 2 combines genomic proximity with matched regulatory evidence to predict likely target genes.
Independent TF-binding and perturbation datasets support these predictions across pancreatic cancer and T-cell systems.
Overall, fp-tools and CraftGRN provide an integrated path from chromatin accessibility, to TF binding, and finally to predicted gene regulation.
These results also point to several future directions.

slides.title: Future Directions
slides.notes_text:
There are 2 main directions for extending this work.
First, we are in active development of CraftGRN Module 3, which focuses on automating the extraction of biologically meaningful GRNs and performing differential GRN analysis across conditions.
Second, we want to extend CraftGRN from condition-level analysis to cell-state-resolved networks using single-cell multiome data, and ultimately apply to spatial single-cell data.
Finally, I’d like to acknowledge the people who made this work possible.

slides.title: Experimental challenges in measuring TF binding
slides.notes_text:
While these The problem is scale.
We have many TFs, but these are targeted assays, so each TF usually needs its own experiment. 
That quickly becomes many experiments, and it also depends on having a good TF-specific antibody. 
More experiments means more time and cost.

slides.title: Gaps in existing ATAC-seq footprinting tools
slides.notes_text:
novelty:
fp-tools extends interpretable TOBIAS-style footprinting into a faster, replicate-aware, single-cell-capable, de novo-motif-aware, and fully reproducible analysis platform.
Compared with the TOBIAS-style baseline, fp-tools adds or extends:
Improved computational efficiency
Faster execution and lower peak memory in the matched benchmark. 
De novo motif discovery integrated with footprint analysis
Candidate footprints can be exported, analyzed with MEME/DREME/STREME, compared with known motifs using Tomtom, and carried back into downstream analysis. 
Biological-replicate differential footprinting
Per-replicate motif scores, replicate summaries, empirical-Bayes moderated testing, and multiple-testing correction rather than treating conditions as single profiles. 
Cross-sample footprint normalization and scaled aggregation
Including shared-background q95 scaling for multi-sample comparisons. 
Integrated pseudobulk single-cell workflow
Grouped scATAC fragments can enter the same core footprint pipeline, with cell-level KNN-smoothed footprint signatures for visualization. 
Interactive and publication-oriented reporting
Interactive HTML reports, linked motif/footprint views, and editable SVG export. 
Reproducible execution surfaces
Command line, saved YAML configurations, browser GUI, run history, and auditable analysis settings. 
Orthogonal validation framework
The full workflow was benchmarked against matched TF ChIP-seq across 12 TF–cell-line comparisons in five cancer cell lines; footprint-score AUROC exceeded PWM AUROC in 10 of 12 comparisons.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers HNF4A binding beyond canonical motif matches
slides.notes_text:
Here I’m showing representative HNF4A loci. The purple track is the independent CUT&Tag signal, the orange marks are canonical motif-supported sites, and the blue marks are CraftGRN predictions.
You can see that CraftGRN recovers many binding sites that are not captured by canonical motif matching alone. This is exactly the advantage we were aiming for: extending TF assignment beyond canonical motif matches while still keeping the predictions anchored to footprint activity and matched TF expression.

slides.title: Footprint signal improves TF-binding prediction
slides.notes_text:
Before showing the comparison, I’ll briefly define the main metrics.
Recall, or true-positive rate, is the fraction of experimentally detected binding sites that we recover. Precision is the fraction of our predictions that are experimentally supported. The false-positive rate measures how often we incorrectly predict binding at negative sites.
In the curves below, blue uses the correlation between TF expression and the broad ATAC-seq signal. Orange uses the correlation with the localized footprint signal.
In both the MAFF and HNF4G benchmarks, the footprint-based approach gives higher true-positive rates and higher precision.
So the localized footprint signal is more informative for TF-binding prediction than accessibility alone.

slides.title: Top footprint-ranked sites contain more true TF-binding predictions
slides.notes_text:
Here I focus only on the top-ranked predictions.
Green represents true positives, and orange represents false positives. As we move from the top 30,000 predictions toward the top 5,000, the footprint-based ranking contains a progressively higher proportion of true positives.
Compared with the ATAC-based ranking, the footprint ranking contains fewer false positives, especially among the highest-ranked sites.
Based on this result, we use footprint activity as the main regulatory signal in the downstream CraftGRN predictions.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers TF-binding sites near epithelial and adaptive-response genes
slides.notes_text:
These tracks show what the predictions look like at individual genomic regions in HPAF-II cells.
Blue is the ATAC-seq signal, purple is the independent TF-specific signal and detected peak calls, orange is CraftGRN, and gray is EPCOT. The gene models below provide the local genomic context.
Across regions near EPCAM, JUP, VIL1, ELF3, EGR1, PCK2, and JAG1, CraftGRN predictions align closely with experimentally detected TF-binding sites.
These genes are associated with epithelial identity, junction organization, stress response, metabolism, and Notch-related signaling.
At this stage, the gene names provide genomic context; the actual target-gene assignment comes later in Module 2.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers multi-TF binding near epithelial and survival genes
slides.notes_text:
We see similar locus-level agreement in AsPC1 across several TF families, including HNF4A, FOSL1, FOSL2, HNF4G, and KLF5.
CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported binding sites near genes associated with epithelial identity and polarity, such as EPCAM, LGALS4, ELF3, PARD6B, and MUC17, as well as adaptive-response genes such as BNIP3L and EGR1.
The key result is agreement at individual binding sites across multiple TFs, rather than only an improvement in aggregate performance.

slides.title: CraftGRN recovers FOSL2 binding near invasion and epithelial genes
slides.notes_text:
This slide focuses on FOSL2 binding in HPAC cells.
CraftGRN recovers experimentally supported sites near genes involved in invasion and remodeling, such as MMP7; metabolic adaptation, such as PCK2; AP-1 feedback, including FOS and JUND; and epithelial adhesion and polarity, including CDH1, CLDN3, CLDN7, and PARD6B.
Again, these are binding-site predictions near biologically relevant genes. They do not yet establish that every nearby gene is directly regulated by FOSL2.
